prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I am so lonely for the twentieth century, for the deeply felt, obscene graffiti of armed men and the beautiful bridges that make them so small and carry them into the hearts of cities written like words across nothing, the dense void history became in my beautiful century. When a man talks reason, he postpones something. He gets in the way of a machine that knows him for the sad vengeance he is, somewhere close to the bald name of his city. "New York" means "strike back." "Attica" means "strike back" and so does anyplace in the world in the huge eyes and tender hands of my century. I went to the capital. I had a banner, and there were thousands of people like me. There was an airplane, and for a moment heavy with laurel and sprays of peach blossom something that has never happened before stretched like a woman's shadow on a hedge between the plane and the people who saw it flying. It was the real name of the century. It told everyone to strike back until there was no reason in the world except a machine stalled overhead that knows everyone and is as delicate as peach blossom. But the poor years come too late.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: When, New, York

outputs.L1:
I am so lonely for the twentieth century—for the deeply felt, obscene graffiti of armed men, and for the beautiful bridges that make them seem so small, carrying them into the hearts of cities written like words across nothing: the dense void that history became in my beautiful century.

When a man speaks of reason, he postpones something. He obstructs a machine that knows him for the sad vengeance he is, somewhere near the stark name of his city. “New York” means “strike back.” “Attica” means “strike back,” and so does every place in the world, in the vast eyes and tender hands of my century.

I went to the capital. I carried a banner, and there were thousands of people like me. There was an airplane, and, for a moment heavy with laurel and sprays of peach blossom, something that had never happened before stretched like a woman’s shadow across a hedge between the plane and the people who watched it fly. It was the true name of the century. It told everyone to strike back until no reason remained in the world—only a machine stalled overhead, a machine that knows everyone and is as delicate as peach blossom.

But the poor years come too late.
outputs.L2:
I ache with longing for the twentieth century: for the raw, profane markings left by men with weapons; for the graceful bridges that dwarf those men while bearing them toward city centers, suspended over emptiness like written language—over the crowded nothingness that history became in my lovely century. Whenever a man appeals to logic, he is delaying an event. He obstructs a machine that recognizes him as a sorrowful act of revenge, somewhere near the stark, unadorned name of his city. “New York” signifies retaliation. “Attica” carries the same command, as does every place on earth, seen through my century’s enormous eyes and held in its gentle hands.

I traveled to the capital carrying a banner, surrounded by thousands who had come as I had. An airplane appeared, and during one moment laden with laurel and branches of peach flowers, an unprecedented thing spread itself—like the silhouette of a woman cast across a hedge—between the aircraft and the crowd watching it pass. That was the century’s true name. It instructed everyone to retaliate until all reason had vanished, leaving only a machine halted in the sky, one that knows every person and possesses the fragility of peach blossom. Yet the years of hardship arrive after their time.
outputs.L3:
The speaker looks back nostalgically on the twentieth century, imagining it as an era marked by a disturbing combination of violence, beauty, and profound historical emptiness. Rather than presenting the period as coherent or morally progressive, the speaker evokes a world in which destruction and aesthetic intensity exist side by side, while history itself seems unable to provide lasting meaning.

Within this vision, cities and politically charged places such as New York and Attica become symbols of resistance. Each location carries the same urgent command: to “strike back.” This repeated imperative suggests that rebellion is not confined to a single event or community but is the century’s defining response to oppression. At the same time, reason is portrayed less as a guide than as an impediment. Reflection delays action and disrupts the cold, impersonal machinery of vengeance, which appears to operate beyond individual judgment or moral hesitation.

During a mass protest in the capital, however, the speaker experiences a brief and unprecedented moment of vision. For an instant, the crowd, an airplane overhead, and delicate images from the natural world seem mysteriously connected. This fleeting perception introduces a fragile beauty into the surrounding atmosphere of political anger and historical violence, suggesting the possibility of unity or transcendence even amid conflict.

Ultimately, the twentieth century’s central message is one of relentless resistance: one must continue to oppose, retaliate, and refuse submission. Yet the conclusion complicates this call to action. The speaker observes that deprivation and hardship arrive “too late,” implying that suffering no longer produces meaningful change or that the historical moment for effective resistance has already passed. The result is a final mood of bitterness and belatedness, in which the demand to fight persists even as its power to transform the world appears uncertain.
outputs.L4:
The speaker presents the twentieth century as an age dominated by violence, machinery, and collective suffering. Rather than describing history in a straightforward narrative, the vision unfolds through surreal, disjointed images: modern cities become threatening landscapes, war intrudes into ordinary life, crowds gather in protest, and an airplane hangs ominously above a mass demonstration. These images blur the boundaries between technological progress and destruction. The airplane, a triumph of modern invention, also embodies surveillance, warfare, and the constant possibility of violence, while the protesting crowd appears trapped beneath the very forces it seeks to oppose.

At the center of this bleak portrait is the idea of retaliation. Individuals, nations, and political movements answer injury with further injury, creating a cycle that seems to define the century itself. Resistance remains necessary, but it is repeatedly delayed or absorbed by the systems against which it struggles. Reason also arrives too late: intellectual understanding may expose the pattern of violence, yet it cannot undo the damage already inflicted. The speaker’s mourning therefore extends beyond particular wars or political disasters. It is a lament for an entire historical era in which human beings have become subordinate to ideologies, institutions, and machines of their own creation. By ending with a sense of belated recognition, the vision suggests that the tragedy of the twentieth century lies not only in its brutality, but also in humanity’s inability to escape the mechanisms of revenge and dehumanization before they become history.
outputs.L5:
### When New York Wakes

When morning reaches New York, the city does not simply wake—it surges into motion. Trains thunder beneath crowded streets, coffee carts send steam into the air, and sunlight flashes across towers of glass. Every corner seems to promise a new beginning.

By nightfall, New York becomes a constellation of windows, headlights, and glowing signs. Yet even in the noise, there are quiet moments: a stranger offering directions, music drifting from an open doorway, or someone standing beneath the skyline and believing, perhaps for the first time, that anything is possible.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem mourning the twentieth century, blending war, protest, cities, machines, and fragile natural imagery in a dense, elegiac voice.
counterfactuals.output:
The century died standing beneath an electric clock, its pockets full of shrapnel, ballot stubs, factory whistles, and photographs of children waving from trains. No one could agree on the hour. In Sarajevo a violin kept sawing at the rain; in Hiroshima, shadows clung to the walls after their bodies had gone; in Berlin, concrete dreamed it was a border and woke beneath hammers, astonished by daylight.

O century of sirens and speeches, your cities wore smoke like mourning veils. Tanks flowered in the squares. Students lifted their bare hands against the black arithmetic of uniforms, and the streets answered with water cannons, slogans, boots, the bright, brief birds of broken glass. From radios came the grainy voices of the dead, still promising bread, victory, freedom, tomorrow—always tomorrow, that locked room at the end of the corridor.

Meanwhile the machines multiplied their metallic angels. Assembly lines carried identical hearts beneath fluorescent suns. Elevators rose through offices where men traded wheat, oil, and distant weather. Computers learned to count our hunger. Satellites circled the planet like sleepless silver moths, transmitting wars into living rooms where blue flowers trembled in porcelain cups.

Yet somewhere, under the helicopter’s enormous shadow, a fox crossed the snow without ideology. A poppy leaned through barbed wire. In a poisoned river, one translucent fish persisted, bearing the moon in its ruined gills. Forests whispered in the old language of rain, though chainsaws translated poorly.

Now the century lies down at last, long as a railway, cold as a monument. We cover it with newspapers, flags, and the soft ash of vanished names. Above it, the new clocks begin their insect ticking. But listen: inside the grave, typewriters still chatter; crowds still sing; a bicycle bell rings in an evacuated city. And from the rubble, impossibly tender, a blade of grass lifts its green antenna, searching the air for news.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical monologue in which a speaker remembers attending a mass demonstration in the capital and interprets an airplane overhead as a symbol of vengeance, history, and political resistance.
counterfactuals.output:
I remember the capital that morning—  
its avenues swollen with footsteps,  
its stone facades listening at last.  
We came from alleys, factories, classrooms,  
from kitchens where the radio whispered,  
from fields whose dust still clung to our shoes.  
We carried no common face, only a common wound,  
and above us the banners moved  
like bright, impatient weather.

Then the airplane crossed the sky.

How small it seemed, a silver thorn  
drawn through the blue—yet every head lifted.  
For one breath the chanting faltered,  
and I thought of all the aircraft history had sent us:  
those that mapped our villages for conquest,  
those that darkened the sun before the bombs,  
those that carried ministers safely away  
while the streets learned the names of the dead.

But this one turned in the light,  
and its wings flashed like a blade being remembered.

I said: Look—vengeance does not always descend as fire.  
Sometimes it is only the past returning overhead,  
circling until the powerful understand  
that nothing is buried merely because they forbid mourning.  
Every prison leaves an echo.  
Every vanished body becomes a witness.  
Every order shouted from a balcony  
is written somewhere beyond the reach of censors.

The airplane passed, but its thunder remained among us.  
It entered our drums, our throats,  
the iron railings trembling beneath our hands.  
We marched toward the square as if toward an old debt,  
not to inherit the tyrant’s cruelty,  
but to collect the future he had stolen.

And I knew then that history was not behind us.  
It was above us, beneath us, inside our steps—  
a vast machine built from memory,  
terrible and unfinished.

We raised our banners higher.

The capital, for all its monuments, looked suddenly mortal.  
The palace windows shone without answering.  
And over their silence our voices climbed,  
following that bright speck into distance,  
until even the sky seemed to carry our refusal.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental paragraph of poetic prose using the recurring phrase “strike back,” references to New York and Attica, and contrasting images of armed men, bridges, machinery, and peach blossoms.
counterfactuals.output: Strike back, says New York in the iron dialect of scaffolds and sirens; strike back, mutters Attica through walls that remember every fist and name. Armed men stand beneath the bridges, their shadows nailed to the river, while machinery grinds on—gears chewing daylight, pistons coughing sparks into the rain. Strike back, the steel insists, but along the fence peach blossoms loosen, pale as small flags of surrender, soft as mouths refusing the language of guns. Above them, the bridges carry thousands home, trembling between violence and mercy; below, the engines turn, the rifles wait, and spring, impossible spring, strikes back.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Imagine someone nostalgically addressing the twentieth century as both beautiful and violent. Write their fragmented meditation on reason, rebellion, technology, public protest, and years that arrive too late.
counterfactuals.output:
O twentieth century—  
beautiful in your smoke,  
violent in your light.

You taught reason to wear a uniform,  
to number the dead,  
to call the number progress.

And still rebellion rose:  
a fist from a factory gate,  
a song smuggled through prison walls,  
students lifting blank pages  
against the enormous grammar of power.

Your machines promised time.  
They gave us speed.  
Your screens promised truth.  
They gave us the bright, repeating wound.

In the public square, bodies became voices.  
The police arrived with shields.  
History arrived with cameras.  
Justice arrived—  
as always—  
after the blood had dried.

We believed the next year would save us.  
Then the next.

Some years came wearing medals.  
Some came carrying sirens.  
The necessary years  
were always delayed at the border.

O beautiful, brutal century,  
you ended without ending.

Even now your engines run beneath our sleep.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a dark, surrealist prose poem about the historical void left by the twentieth century, with long associative sentences, personified cities, an ominous stalled airplane, and a final note of belated sorrow.
counterfactuals.output:
The twentieth century departed without closing the door, and through that black, revolving aperture came the smell of wet uniforms, burnt ledgers, hospital soap, and winter wheat crushed beneath machines whose names had been filed smooth by tribunals, while the clocks in abandoned ministries continued to stamp the same hour upon the dust, as if time itself had been arrested at a border and ordered to surrender its papers.

Berlin woke nightly with iron teeth in her mouth; Sarajevo kept a bullet beneath her tongue; Warsaw, thin and sleepless, counted her vanished children by touching the cold bricks where their shadows had been bricked in; Hiroshima wore a white dress no rain could wash, and far to the east and west the other cities muttered in their ruined sleep, each blaming the rivers, each begging the rivers to remember what the maps had agreed to forget.

Above them an airplane hung motionless in a sky the color of old film, its propellers stalled, its windows lit by a pale interior noon, and inside sat passengers who had been dead for decades without being informed, holding newspapers whose headlines crawled like insects from war to war, while the pilot listened through his headphones for a command from the future and heard only the ocean chewing patiently on its wreckage.

Beneath that impossible aircraft, parades crossed empty squares, statues raised their stone arms to hail no one, factories exhaled the names of the disappeared, and history—blindfolded, perfumed, carrying a suitcase full of teeth—wandered from checkpoint to checkpoint asking which century this was, though every guard had already been replaced by a mirror.

We inherited the void as one inherits a locked room in a condemned house: with gratitude rehearsed for the lawyers, with terror hidden from the children, with the key growing warmer each year in the palm; and only now, so late that even the dead have ceased expecting us, do we kneel before the door and call what we feel sorrow.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
